card.keepWhy: Too small to matter? Rama didn’t think so.
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda: Rama’s army, with the builder Nala, builds the bridge of stones across the ocean to Lanka
The squirrel’s help and its three stripes: a folk story told across India, especially in the South (the film’s note: not in Valmiki’s Ramayana)
check: Where the squirrel story is first found (often credited to South Indian retellings and oral tradition); confirm the source line “a folk story.”

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? ever feel like your part is too small to matter? one person, one voice, one tiny try.
options: then this little one is for you. listen.
then keep this one for those days. listen.
good. you’ll love this sweet one anyway.

steps.line: Rama’s army was building a bridge of stones across the ocean. Giant monkeys and bears hauled huge boulders.
And a little squirrel wanted to help too.
steps.label: a folk story

steps.q: The squirrel can’t lift a single stone. How do you guess it helps build the bridge?
o: It cheers the monkeys on from the shore
It carries tiny pebbles in its mouth
It fills the gaps with sand
steps.why: Sand, one tiny load at a time, to fill the gaps. Watch.

steps.line: It rolled in the sand, ran onto the bridge, and shook the sand off between the stones. Again, and again.
steps.label: a folk story

steps.q: The squirrel is one of the best-loved Ramayana stories. Where does it come from?
steps.why: It isn’t in Valmiki’s Ramayana. It grew up in later tellings across India, and families have passed it on for centuries.

steps.q: The monkeys laugh at the squirrel. What do you think Rama does?
o: Sends it home where it’s safe
steps.why: He picks it up, gently. Of everyone on that bridge, Rama notices the smallest helper.

steps.line: Rama didn’t. He picked the squirrel up and gently stroked its back. And that, the story says, is why Indian squirrels have three stripes.
steps.label: a folk story

steps.q: Why didn’t Rama laugh like the monkeys?
o: He saw the love in the effort, not its size
He thought the sand would hold the bridge up
He felt sorry for the little thing
steps.why: Rama looked at the heart behind the help. In this story, a small offering made with love is never small to him.

steps.line: Small efforts count. Two minutes a day, again and again, adds up.
steps.label: today

steps.q: You only have two minutes today. What would the squirrel do?
o: Skip it; two minutes won’t matter
Wait for a day with a free hour
Do the two minutes, come back tomorrow
steps.why: One load of sand fills nothing; load after load fills the gaps. That’s how the smallest helper built part of a bridge.

say: here’s what i love. the squirrel couldn’t lift a single stone. rama still saw it.
many hindus tell this story to say god looks at the love in what you offer, not its size. a tiny effort, given with your whole heart, counts.

steps.q: The monkeys had a master builder. In Valmiki’s Ramayana, who designed the bridge?
o: Nala, son of the gods’ architect
steps.why: Nala, son of Vishvakarma, builds it (Yuddha Kanda 22). The great epic credits the engineer; the folk tellings gave the smallest helper a place too.

today.say: today, pick one tiny thing you can offer, two minutes a day: a page, a call, a dish washed for someone. many hindus offer small acts to god with a quiet “shri ram.” you can say it, or just do the thing with love. it’s your choice.
options: then roll in the sand. two minutes, again and again.
so was the squirrel’s. rama picked it up anyway.
